items.stem: Which term describes the subjects and content that schools officially teach and assess?
items.answer: Formal curriculum
items.markingKey: Formal curriculum: the subjects and content that schools officially teach and assess. [1]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “stratification of knowledge”? Give one example.
items.answer: The ranking of some kinds of knowledge as higher status than others. Example: academic subjects valued above vocational ones.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (the ranking of some kinds of knowledge as higher status than others); 1 mark for a relevant example such as academic subjects valued above vocational ones. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “national curriculum” and “stratification of knowledge”, using an example of each.
items.answer: National curriculum: a curriculum set by the state that all state schools must follow (e.g. compulsory subjects up to age 16). Stratification of knowledge: the ranking of some kinds of knowledge as higher status than others (e.g. academic subjects valued above vocational ones).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: The government in Kathmandu makes coding compulsory for all pupils but removes art and drama from the core curriculum. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: education reproduces class inequality and legitimates it: the hidden curriculum prepares working-class pupils for subordinate jobs (Bowles and Gintis), schools act as ideological state apparatuses (Althusser), and the myth of meritocracy makes failure seem the individual’s fault.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: In a school in Madrid, pupils who take vocational courses are taught in a separate building and cannot study the subjects needed for university. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: education performs vital functions for society: it passes on shared values and creates social solidarity (Durkheim), acts as a bridge from particularistic family values to universalistic values of wider society, and allocates people to roles on the basis of merit (Parsons, Davis and Moore).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of case studies for studying the hidden curriculum of school rules and routines.
items.answer: Strengths: they can be used to generate hypotheses that are tested later on larger samples; they may use several methods, increasing validity. Limitations: the researcher’s interpretation may be biased; the detailed data is difficult to compare with other cases. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the hidden curriculum of school rules and routines but best combined with another method such as laboratory experiments (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: In a school in Bangkok, pupils who take vocational courses are taught in a separate building and cannot study the subjects needed for university. Compare how functionalist and Marxist sociologists might interpret this situation.

Marxism: education reproduces class inequality and legitimates it: the hidden curriculum prepares working-class pupils for subordinate jobs (Bowles and Gintis), schools act as ideological state apparatuses (Althusser), and the myth of meritocracy makes failure seem the individual’s fault.

items.stem: Explain two features of the hidden curriculum.
items.answer: Hierarchy and authority; punctuality and routine; competition and individualism; gender messages; acceptance of boredom; correspondence with work (Bowles and Gintis).

items.stem: What is meant by the term “cultural reproduction”? Give one example.
items.answer: The passing on of the dominant culture through education, reproducing inequality. Example: schools rewarding the culture of the dominant group.

items.stem: Distinguish between “ethnocentric curriculum” and “multicultural education”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Ethnocentric curriculum: a curriculum that reflects one culture and ignores or marginalises others (e.g. literature syllabuses with only majority-group authors). Multicultural education: education that recognises and values the cultures of all pupils (e.g. teaching about the festivals of several religions).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A campaign group in Accra calls for the school history syllabus to include the experiences of colonised peoples and migrants. Suggest how a postmodernist sociologist might explain this.

items.stem: In Accra, the only language other than the national language offered at school is French, although many pupils speak Urdu, Tamil or Arabic at home. Explain how a postmodernist sociologist might interpret this situation.

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using unstructured interviews to research representations of different cultures in school textbooks.
items.answer: Strengths: they allow people to explain the meanings they give to their experiences in their own words; rapport between interviewer and interviewee builds trust, so people may reveal more, producing valid data. Limitations: each interview is unique, so it is hard to repeat and the data is less reliable; they are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying representations of different cultures in school textbooks but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: What is the difference between “decolonising the curriculum” and “multicultural education”?

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “gatekeeper”, and give one example.
items.answer: A person who controls access to a research setting, such as a head teacher. Example: a head teacher deciding whether a researcher may observe lessons.

items.stem: Distinguish between “peer pressure in research” and “school documents”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Peer pressure in research: the tendency of pupils to answer in ways that impress their peers in group interviews (e.g. boys exaggerating anti-school attitudes in front of friends). School documents: official records produced by schools, such as reports, policies and exclusion records (e.g. inspection reports and pupil records).

items.stem: A researcher in Colombo wants to interview 14-year-olds about bullying, using groups of five friends at a time. Suggest how a feminist sociologist might view this research.

items.stem: A researcher in Singapore wants to interview 14-year-olds about bullying, using groups of five friends at a time. Explain how an interpretivist sociologist might evaluate this research.

items.stem: Tariq is planning a study of pupils’ experiences of bullying. Evaluate the use of field experiments for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: variables in a school, such as teacher expectations, can be altered in a normal classroom; participants usually do not know they are part of an experiment, so they act naturally. Limitations: deceiving people about sensitive matters may cause harm or distress; participants have not given informed consent, which raises ethical issues. Theory: field experiments are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ experiences of bullying but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using case studies to research pupils’ experiences of bullying.
items.answer: Strengths: a single case can give rare insight into an unusual or closed group; they give a detailed, in-depth picture of one group, institution or community. Limitations: the researcher’s interpretation may be biased; one case may be untypical, so findings cannot be generalised. Theory: case studies are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce mainly qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ experiences of bullying but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: “Qualitative methods are the most useful for studying education.” Evaluate this view.
items.answer: For: Observation and interviews reveal labelling, subcultures and meanings (Willis, Ball, Lacey, Fuller); validity; interactionist preference. Against: Official statistics show national patterns (Gillborn uses data); questionnaires reach large samples; qualitative studies are small and hard to generalise; ethical and access problems with pupils; mixed methods. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement on how far the view holds.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): a few simple points. Level 2 (4-6): some explained arguments, mainly on one side; limited evaluation. Level 3 (7-9): a range of explained arguments and evidence for and against, with some evaluation. Level 4 (10-12): a balanced, well-supported analysis using theories, studies and concepts, sustained evaluation and a reasoned conclusion. For: Observation and interviews reveal labelling, subcultures and meanings (Willis, Ball, Lacey, Fuller); validity; interactionist preference. items.stem: Bernstein argued that the way knowledge is classified and framed shapes pupils’ experience of school. Explain this view and one criticism of it.

items.stem: The government in Seoul makes coding compulsory for all pupils but removes art and drama from the core curriculum. Suggest how a liberal feminist sociologist might explain this.

items.stem: Yusuf is planning a study of which subjects pupils see as most valuable. Explain two limitations of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: 1. They cannot measure patterns across a large population because only a few people can be interviewed. 2. They are time-consuming and the data is hard to analyse and compare.

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of official statistics for studying which subjects pupils see as most valuable.
items.answer: Strengths: they give national data on whole populations that no single researcher could collect; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they cannot tell us how people feel or why they act as they do; interpretivists argue they are social constructions shaped by the decisions of officials and the public. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying which subjects pupils see as most valuable but best combined with another method such as personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Assess how useful structured interviews are for studying teacher labelling in classrooms.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; every respondent is asked the same questions in the same order, so results are standardised and reliable. items.stem: In Karachi, the only language other than the national language offered at school is French, although many pupils speak Urdu, Tamil or Arabic at home. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: a shared curriculum promotes social solidarity and integration into a common national culture (Durkheim).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Assess how useful content analysis is for studying representations of different cultures in school textbooks.
items.answer: Strengths: media content from different decades can be compared to measure change; it is cheap and the sources (newspapers, television, websites) are easy to obtain. Limitations: counting does not reveal the meanings audiences take from the content; it shows what content contains but not how audiences interpret it. Theory: content analysis is favoured by positivist (quantitative content analysis) or interpretivist (qualitative content analysis) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying representations of different cultures in school textbooks but best combined with another method such as self-completion questionnaires (triangulation).

Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a person who controls access to a research setting, such as a head teacher?
items.answer: Gatekeeper
items.markingKey: Gatekeeper: a person who controls access to a research setting, such as a head teacher. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “gatekeeper”.
items.answer: A person who controls access to a research setting, such as a head teacher.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: a person who controls access to a research setting, such as a head teacher. [1]

items.stem: Explain two problems of using participant observation to study classrooms.
items.answer: Gaining access through gatekeepers; adults cannot easily pass as pupils, so observation is usually overt and the Hawthorne effect is likely; teachers may change their behaviour; time-consuming; small samples.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each explained problem. [4]

items.stem: A sociologist in Cairo wants to research national patterns of educational achievement. Explain one limitation of using longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) for this research.
items.answer: They are very expensive and results take many years to appear.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of national patterns of educational achievement. [2]

items.stem: A researcher spends a year in a school in Nairobi, attending lessons and joining pupils at lunchtimes. Which research method is being used?
items.answer: Participant observation
items.markingKey: Participant observation: the researcher takes part in the life of the group. [1]

items.stem: Kenji plans to sit at the back of Year 9 lessons in a school in Kathmandu for a term, counting how often teachers praise boys and girls. Suggest how a feminist sociologist might view this research.
items.answer: Feminism: research should give a voice to pupils whose experiences are overlooked, such as girls, and use sensitive, non-hierarchical methods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Assess how useful semi-structured interviews are for studying teacher labelling in classrooms.
items.answer: Strengths: open follow-up questions let interviewees explain their reasoning; they are more flexible than structured interviews but easier to analyse than unstructured ones. Limitations: follow-up questions differ between interviews, so reliability is lower than with a fixed schedule; samples are usually fairly small, so representativeness is limited. Theory: semi-structured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative and quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying teacher labelling in classrooms but best combined with another method such as official statistics (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using official statistics to research national patterns of educational achievement.
items.answer: Strengths: regular collection over many years allows long-term trends to be identified; they are collected regularly, so trends over time and comparisons between groups can be made. Limitations: they are collected for government purposes, so categories may not fit the sociologist’s needs; definitions and methods of collection may change over time, making comparisons difficult. Theory: official statistics are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying national patterns of educational achievement but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
